## **Reduce your inference cost by almost half, on a single GPU with vLLM**


*Acknowledgements: thanks to*[Amit Sehgal](https://www.linkedin.com/in/imamitsehgal/) *and*[Satendra Kumar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/satendrakumar06/) *for contributing to this blog.*


Google’s[Gemma 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02770) family is one of the strongest open model releases so far. The largest dense model, **Gemma-4–31B-it** , ranks as the top open dense model on the Arena text leaderboard (Elo 1451). It comes under the Apache 2.0 license, so you can run it, fine-tune it, and ship it however you like.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*Arena text Elo vs. model size. Source:*[Google DeepMind, Gemma 4](https://deepmind.google/models/gemma/gemma-4/) *.*


Inside the bank, we’re fine-tuning Gemma 4 on our own data for multilingual customer conversations, many of them in Indic languages. That’s a story for another post. This one is about the engineering underneath it: how we tuned the serving stack so the same GPU serves far more tokens, and the cost of every token drops sharply.


Before getting into the tuning, here’s what makes the model worth the effort.


## Meet Gemma-4–31B-it


**Advanced reasoning.** Gemma 4 has a built-in *thinking mode* . Turn it on, and the model writes out a reasoning trace before it answers. With thinking enabled, the 31B model scores:


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**Built-in speculative decoding (MTP).** Google also ships a small **multi-token prediction (MTP) drafter** with Gemma 4. It’s a 4-layer, ~500M-parameter model that reuses the main model’s KV cache to guess several tokens ahead. vLLM supports it directly, and in Step 5 below it gives us **+45% throughput** on its own.


**Efficient long-context design.** Most layers use local sliding-window attention, with one global-attention layer for every five local ones. Global layers also reuse keys as values. Together, these cut the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, which matters a lot when you serve 16K-token prompts on a single GPU.


**Ready for agents.** Native function calling and tool use are built in. The 31B model scores 75.0 / 86.4 / 69.3 on the Tau2 airline / retail / telecom agent benchmarks.


*All numbers above come from the*[Gemma 4 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02770) *.*


## Why an open model instead of a managed API


**1. Nobody can retire it on you.** A model you host keeps running until *you* decide to change it. Managed APIs don’t make that promise. For example, Gemini-2.5-Flash has been deprecated and removed from Google AI Studio, and from **December 1, 2026** , its API calls will be routed to Gemini-3.5-Flash-Lite and billed at Flash-Lite rates.


**2. You can fine-tune it.** Gemma’s weights are open, so we can fine-tune it on our own data and own the result, which is exactly what we’re doing in-house. Gemini is a closed API model.


**3. Your data stays private.** The model runs in our own GKE cluster, so no prompt leaves our VPC. For a bank handling customer conversations, that matters.


**4. It’s much cheaper at steady load.** Enterprises like ours usually buy Gemini on Vertex AI through **Provisioned Throughput** : a fixed monthly price per Generative AI Scale Unit (GSU), about **$2,000 + taxes** each, for a fixed number of tokens per second. To match what one tuned GPU serves on our workload, you would need:


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


That’s **half the cost of Gemini-2.5-Flash** and **about 5.3× cheaper than Gemini-3.5-Flash** . The full breakdown is further down.


> ***A note on the Gemini comparison:*** *Gemini Flash is here only as a price reference. It may well be a bigger and more capable general-purpose model. But for our specific tasks, Gemma-4–31B-it works very well, so this is purely a cost comparison, not a claim about which model is better.*


## Why Gemma-4–31B-it and not another open model?


Before choosing Gemma-4–31B-it, we evaluated three similar-sized open models: two Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, **Gemma-4–26B-A4B-it** and **Qwen-3.6–35B-A3B** , and one dense model, **Qwen3.8–27B** .


- **Dense vs. MoE:** An MoE model activates only a small part of its weights for each token. For example, “A4B” means about 4B active parameters out of 26B. That makes MoE models fast and cheap, but each token gets less of the model’s capacity. A dense model like Gemma-4–31B-it uses **all 31B parameters for every token** , which helps on harder tasks that need more nuance.
- **Gemma vs. Qwen dense:** Qwen3.8–27B is also dense and close in size, so the difference there comes from the training data rather than the architecture. Gemma’s broad multilingual training gives it the edge on Indic languages.
- **Multilingual and Indic language understanding:** Our use case involves multiple languages, especially Indic languages. In our internal evaluations, **Gemma-4–31B-it beat all three models by a clear margin** and came **close to Gemini-2.5-Flash accuracy** .


**The trade-off:** that accuracy comes with a serving cost, which we cover in the next section. We wanted dense-model accuracy at a cost that still beats a managed API.


## Cost breakdown: self-hosted Gemma vs. Gemini


**How Provisioned Throughput is measured.** Each GSU gives a fixed number of tokens per second, but output tokens count several times over (Google calls this the *burndown rate* ). You can only buy whole GSUs.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**What one GPU serves.** On our benchmark workload (16K input / 512 output per request), the tuned server handles **5,387 input + 168 output tokens/sec** . Converted to GSU terms:


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**Before vs. after tuning.** Running 24/7 for a 30-day month (2,592,000 seconds):


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Against Gemini-3.5-Flash, the tuned GPU saves about **$13,000 a month** .


**The tuning is what makes the numbers work.** With vLLM’s default settings, one GPU did less than a single Gemini-2.5-Flash GSU and cost 1.5× as much. After tuning, it does the work of three GSUs at half their price.


> ***Caveats: Both sides are flat-rate.*** *A GSU costs the same busy or idle, just like the GPU, so utilization doesn’t change the comparison.* ***Rounding matters.*** *GSUs come in whole units. Against the exact 2.57 GSUs, the tuned GPU is about 1.7× cheaper than Gemini-2.5-Flash rather than 2×.* ***Thinking tokens burn at the output rate.*** *Turning on Gemini’s thinking mode would raise the GSUs needed further.* ***Caching helps both sides.*** *Provisioned Throughput counts cached input at a fraction of the normal rate (0.1× on Gemini-3.5-Flash), which suits a voice bot’s repeated history. vLLM’s prefix caching gives Gemma a similar benefit that our random-prompt benchmark doesn’t capture.* ***Taxes and ops aren’t included.*** *Prices are compared pre-tax, and the GPU figure doesn’t include the engineering time to run it.*


## The inherent challenge of a 31B dense model


The density that makes Gemma-4–31B-it accurate is the same thing that makes it slow. Three reasons:


- **Every token reads every weight.** A dense model uses all 31B parameters for every token it generates. In bf16 that’s about 64 GB of weights streamed from GPU memory on each decode step. At the RTX PRO 6000’s ~1.6–1.8 TB/s of memory bandwidth (depending on the edition), that alone sets a floor of roughly 35–40 ms per step, before attention or scheduling overhead. A 4B-active MoE model reads about 8× less per token.
- **Long prompts are expensive to read.** Prefill costs about 2 FLOPs per parameter per input token. A 16K-token prompt on a 31B model is about 1 PFLOP of matrix math (2 × 31B × 16,384) before the first output token appears, and the user feels all of it as TTFT.
- **The weights crowd out the KV cache.** 64 GB of weights on a 96 GB card leaves well under a third of the memory for the KV cache, activations, and everything else. Only a handful of 16K-token conversations fit on the GPU at once, so the rest wait in a queue.


Out of the box, that’s exactly what we saw: with vLLM’s default settings, the server managed **~1,600 tokens/sec** , and users waited **~40 seconds** for the first token. For a voice bot, 40 seconds of silence is a dropped call.


None of this is a bug. It’s the price of density, and the job is to work around it without giving up the accuracy we chose the model for.


## Our approach: know your use case first


Before touching a single flag, pin down the shape of your traffic. The same model on the same GPU needs different tuning depending on how many tokens go in and how many come out, because the two halves of inference stress different parts of the GPU:


- **Prefill** (reading the input) is compute-bound and drives **TTFT** .
- **Decode** (writing the output, one token at a time) is memory-bandwidth-bound and drives **TPOT** .


Three common use cases show how different that can look:


Press enter or click to view image in full size


A few details matter more than they first appear:


- **A voice bot re-sends the whole conversation on every turn.** Turn 10 carries the system prompt plus nine turns of history, so input keeps growing while output stays small. With prefix caching, only the new part needs prefill. Without it, you pay for the same 8K system prompt on every turn.
- **Voice is latency-first.** TTFT is the silence before the bot starts speaking, so it matters more than raw throughput. Once the bot is talking, decode only has to stay ahead of speech, which is a few tokens per second.
- **Text chat has a long tail on output.** Most answers are short, but a single 4,096-token table holds a decode slot for a long time. Size the context window and batching for that tail, not the average.
- **Document extraction needs the vision encoder.** You can’t skip it with` --language-model-only` , so less memory is left for the KV cache, and the workload is heavy on both prefill and decode.


**Ours is primarily a voice bot.** That’s why every benchmark in this post uses a long-input, short-output shape, and why we watch TTFT as closely as throughput.


## Initial setup and benchmarking harness


Every number in this post comes from the same harness: one GPU, one fixed workload, one benchmark command, and one flag changed at a time.


We run vLLM inside a GKE cluster on a node pool with one RTX PRO 6000 GPU:


```text
gcloud beta container node-pools create ...
```


## Workload profile


Every benchmark below uses the same workload, sized to match our voice bot traffic:


- **Input:** 16,384 tokens per request, above the typical 10–12K so the numbers hold for longer calls
- **Output:** 512 tokens per request, the top of our per-turn range
- **Concurrency:** 8 requests in flight
- **Total:** 100 prompts


> *This is a* ***long-input, short-output*** *workload, so most of the GPU’s work is prefill. The benchmark also sends random prompts, so prefix caching gets almost no hits. Real voice traffic, where each turn shares the previous turn’s prefix, should do better than the numbers here. If your traffic looks like text chat or document extraction, change the benchmark parameters to match it.*


## Baseline deployment


Gemma-4–31B-it supports a 256K context window by default, but its KV cache won’t fit on a single RTX PRO 6000 at that length. We start with 32K and leave every other setting at vLLM’s defaults.

` deploy.yaml` (trimmed to the relevant part):


```text
apiVersion: apps/v1  kind: Deployment  metadata:    name: text-llm-server    namespace: dev-vllm  spec:    template:      spec:        containers:          - name: vllm            args:              - >                vllm serve                --host 0.0.0.0                --port 8080                --model /models/gemma-4-31B-it                --served-model-name gemma-4-31B-it                --enable-prefix-caching                --enable-chunked-prefill                --enable-auto-tool-choice                --async-scheduling                --language-model-only                --tool-call-parser gemma4                --chat-template examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja                --reasoning-parser gemma4                --trust-remote-code                --max-model-len 32768
```


## What the baseline flags do


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Deploy it and wait for the pod to become ready, which takes about 5 minutes while the weights load:


```text
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml  kubectl -n dev-vllm get pod -w  kubectl -n dev-vllm logs -f <pod-name>
```


One line in the startup log is worth pointing out:


```text
Gemma4 model has heterogeneous head dimensions {'sliding_attention': 256, 'full_attention': 512}.  FA4 not available, forcing TRITON_ATTN backend.
```


Gemma 4 uses two different attention head sizes. The FlashAttention-4 kernels can’t handle that combination on this GPU, so vLLM falls back to the slower Triton attention backend. We revisit this in Step 6.


## Running the benchmark


We use vLLM’s built-in benchmark tool from inside the pod:


```text
kubectl -n dev-vllm exec -it <pod-name> -- bash
```


```text
vllm bench serve \    --model /models/gemma-4-31B-it \    --served-model-name gemma-4-31B-it \    --backend openai-chat \    --base-url http://localhost:8080 \    --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \    --random-input-len 16384 \    --random-output-len 512 \    --max-concurrency 8 \    --num-prompts 100
```


## How we run each experiment


1. Change **one** flag in` deploy.yaml` .
2. Redeploy and wait for the pod to become ready.
3. Run the identical` vllm bench serve` command above.
4. Record throughput, TTFT, TPOT, and ITL, and keep the change only if it helps.


## Baseline results


```text
============ Serving Benchmark Result ============  Successful requests:                     100  Benchmark duration (s):                  1059.78  Total token throughput (tok/s):          1595.56  Output token throughput (tok/s):         48.31  ---------------Time to First Token----------------  Mean TTFT (ms):                          39638.24  Median TTFT (ms):                        46601.69  P99 TTFT (ms):                           55015.58  -----Time per Output Token (excl. 1st token)------  Mean TPOT (ms):                          82.59  ---------------Inter-token Latency----------------  Mean ITL (ms):                           84.69  ==================================================
```


**1,596 tokens/sec, and users wait almost 40 seconds for the first token.** We can do much better.


> ***Reading the metrics Total token throughput:*** *input + output tokens processed per second. Higher is better.* ***TTFT (Time To First Token):*** *how long a user waits before the response starts. Lower is better.* ***TPOT (Time Per Output Token):*** *how fast tokens stream once generation starts. Lower is better.* ***ITL (Inter-Token Latency):*** *the gap between consecutive streamed chunks the client receives. Lower is better.*


## Let’s start the real game of optimization


With the harness in place, we changed seven settings, one at a time. The order is deliberate: first free up memory for the KV cache (Steps 1–3), then check batching (Step 4), then cut the cost of every decoded token (Steps 5–7).


## The scoreboard


Here’s where we ended up on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell, 96 GB): total throughput went from **1,596 to 5,555 tokens/sec (3.48×)** , and mean TTFT fell from **39.6 s to 3.8 s (−90%)** . All 100 requests succeeded in every run.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*Each step changes one flag. Percentages are relative to the previous step.*


Each step below covers what the setting does, why it helps, and what it did to our numbers.


## Step 1: Shrink the context window to what you actually need


**What it does:**` --max-model-len` sets the longest sequence (prompt + output) the server will accept. Our requests never go over 16,384 + 512 = 16,896 tokens, so we set it to **20,480** to leave some headroom.


**Why it helps:** vLLM sizes some of its memory reservations around the worst-case sequence length. A smaller limit leaves more GPU memory for the KV cache, so more requests fit on the GPU at once and fewer wait in the queue.


```text
- --max-model-len 32768  + --max-model-len 20480
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## Step 2: Give vLLM more GPU memory


Here’s` nvidia-smi` during the previous run:


```text
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blac...  | 578W / 600W | 88601MiB / 97887MiB | 100% |
```


vLLM’s default memory budget is 90% of the GPU, which leaves about 9 GB unused.


**What it does:**` --gpu-memory-utilization` sets the fraction of GPU memory vLLM may use for model weights, activations, and the KV cache. Raising it to **0.95** gives that extra memory to the KV cache.


**Why it helps:** More KV cache lets more 16K-token prompts sit on the GPU at the same time, so requests spend less time queued. That’s why TTFT drops so sharply. Keep a little headroom, because setting it too close to 1.0 can cause out-of-memory errors.


```text
+ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


> *With more requests decoding at once, each token takes slightly longer (higher TPOT). For this prefill-heavy workload, that’s a good trade.*


## Step 3: Store the KV cache in FP8


**What it does:**` --kv-cache-dtype fp8` stores the attention key/value cache in 8-bit floats instead of the model's 16-bit` bfloat16` . The model weights themselves stay in` bfloat16` .


**Why it helps:** Each cached token takes **half the memory** , so the KV cache holds about twice as many tokens and the attention kernels read half as many bytes. Blackwell GPUs support FP8 in hardware, and the effect on quality is usually negligible.


```text
+ --dtype bfloat16          # default, listed for clarity  + --kv-cache-dtype fp8
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## Step 4: Tune batching (no gain this time)


vLLM uses **continuous batching** : new requests join the running batch at every step instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish. Two settings control how big that batch can get:


- ` **--max-num-seqs**` **:** the maximum number of requests processed together in one step. A higher value allows more parallelism but needs more memory.
- ` **--max-num-batched-tokens**` **:** the maximum number of tokens (prefill chunks + decode tokens) processed in one step. Larger chunks keep the GPU busier during prefill but can slow down decoding for other requests.


```text
+ --max-num-seqs 16  + --max-num-batched-tokens 8192
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**Why there was no change:** The startup log shows` max_num_batched_tokens=8192` was already the default, and our benchmark never sends more than 8 requests at a time, so allowing 16 sequences has no effect. We also tried` --max-num-seqs 32 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384` and saw no improvement. These settings matter more at higher concurrency.


## Step 5: Speculative decoding 🚀


**What it does:**[Speculative decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318) uses a small, fast “draft” model to guess the next few tokens. The large model then checks all of those guesses in a **single** forward pass, so every correct guess is a token we get without a separate pass of the 31B model.


**Why it helps:** Decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because each token requires reading all 31B parameters. Checking 4 guesses costs about the same as generating 1 token. Here we use Gemma’s assistant model as the MTP (multi-token prediction) drafter, proposing 4 tokens at a time.


```text
+ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp", "model":"/models/google__gemma-4-31b-it-assistant", "num_speculative_tokens":4}'
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


** Higher mean ITL is expected here. With speculative decoding, each streamed chunk contains several tokens, so the gaps between chunks get longer even though tokens are generated faster overall (TPOT −30%).*


**How good were the guesses?**


```text
Acceptance rate (%):          62.90  Acceptance length:            3.52    # avg tokens per step  Per-position acceptance (%):  82.6 → 67.0 → 55.1 → 46.9
```


On average, each verification step of the large model produces **3.5 tokens instead of 1** . Acceptance drops for later positions in the guess, so you can also try` num_speculative_tokens` = 2 or 3. For our workload, 4 worked best.


## Step 6: Try the FlashInfer attention backend


Remember the startup warning: FA4 isn’t available, so vLLM falls back to Triton attention. Let’s try FlashInfer instead.


**What it does:**` --attention-backend` chooses which kernel library computes attention. **FlashInfer** provides optimized kernels for both prefill and decode, with good support for paged and FP8 KV caches.


**Why it might help:** Attention takes a large share of the work for 16K-token prompts, so a faster kernel mainly shortens prefill, which shows up as lower TTFT.


```text
+ --attention-backend FLASHINFER
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


TTFT improved somewhat, but throughput stayed flat. Keep this setting if TTFT matters to you, but benchmark it on your own workload before deciding.


## Step 7: FP8 weight quantization (the biggest single win)


**What it does:**` --quantization fp8` converts the model weights from 16-bit to 8-bit floats when the model loads. No separate pre-quantized checkpoint is needed.


**Why it helps:** The weights shrink from about 64 GB to about 32 GB. That **halves the memory read for every decoded token** , lets Blackwell’s FP8 Tensor Cores do the matrix math, and frees roughly 30 GB more for the KV cache.


**The trade-off:** accuracy. On our internal evaluation set, quality dropped by **about 1%** , which is acceptable for our use case. Run your own evals before turning this on.


```text
+ --quantization fp8
```


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## Final configuration


```text
vllm serve \    --host 0.0.0.0 \    --port 8080 \    --model /models/gemma-4-31B-it \    --served-model-name gemma-4-31B-it \    --enable-prefix-caching \    --enable-chunked-prefill \    --enable-auto-tool-choice \    --async-scheduling \    --language-model-only \    --tool-call-parser gemma4 \    --chat-template examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja \    --reasoning-parser gemma4 \    --trust-remote-code \    --max-model-len 20480 \    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \    --dtype bfloat16 \    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \    --quantization fp8 \    --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp", "model":"/models/google__gemma-4-31b-it-assistant", "num_speculative_tokens":4}' \    --attention-backend FLASHINFER
```


## Before vs. after


Press enter or click to view image in full size


> ***Note on inter-token latency (ITL):*** *Mean ITL went up from 84.7 ms to 137.1 ms, but median and P99 ITL both improved. This is a side effect of speculative decoding: tokens arrive in bursts of several at a time, so the gaps between bursts are longer even though overall generation is much faster (as TPOT shows).*


## Key takeaways


1. **Free up memory for the KV cache first.** A right-sized context window, a higher memory budget, and an FP8 KV cache together raised throughput by **1.6×** and cut TTFT by **79%** , with no accuracy cost.
2. **Speculative decoding is the biggest no-accuracy-cost gain** : **+45%** throughput, with each large-model pass producing 3.5 tokens.
3. **FP8 weight quantization adds another +50%** , at the cost of about 1% accuracy. Make the decision based on your own evals.
4. **Not every setting helps.** Batching settings and the attention backend made little difference for this workload, so always benchmark before adopting a change.
5. **Know your use case, and benchmark its real shape.** These results are for a voice bot shape: 16K input, 512 output, concurrency 8. A text-chat or document-extraction workload, with longer outputs, will respond differently to the same settings. Decode-side changes like speculative decoding and FP8 weights are likely to matter even more there.


## What’s next: going to scale


Everything in this post runs on a single GPU. We’re now taking this to a large-scale deployment, and that brings a new set of problems, and new tricks, beyond what one server can show.


Our next post goes into the more advanced techniques we’re building for even faster inference:


- **Prefill/decode disaggregation:** running prefill and decode on separate GPUs, so long voice-bot prompts don’t slow down token generation for calls that are already talking.
- **EPP (Endpoint Picker) routing:** sending each request to the replica best placed to serve it, based on load and what’s already in its KV cache, instead of plain round-robin.
